newsitem.title: GERMANY: Schering raises outlook after record result.
newsitem.headline: Schering raises outlook after record result.

text.p: German drugs group Schering AG raised its forecasts for 1997 results on Wednesday, saying stronger growth in some products should more than offset the cost of takeovers made last year.
Schering said that 1996 profits soared 46 percent to 362 million marks ($216 million) with sales climbing 13 percent to 5.272 billion marks.

"For 1997, at current exchange rates, we expect a 14 percent rise in sales to around six billion marks" with profits rising between 10 and 15 percent, finance chief Klaus Pohle told a news conference.

Pohle said these forecasts, topping his own prediction of four weeks ago that 1997 sales would rise 12 percent with profits growing nine percent, included good-will writeoffs of about 70 million marks for recently-made acquisitions.

The first two months already showed strong sales growth, Pohle said. But he cautioned that the comparison with early 1996 was skewed as Schering acquired the Finnish group Leiras and German group Jenapharm only later in 1996.

Investors were delighted with Schering's stronger outlook, particularly when several other German drugs makers delivered more subdued forecasts. Its shares rose by over one percent during bourse trade.
Profit-taking, however, knocked the shares lower again and they closed at the day's low, up five pfennigs at 156.25 marks. The DAX index closed up 0.75 percent.

Schering, the world's biggest maker of oral contraceptives, said growth would be largely due to higher sales of fertility and hormone drugs as well as therapeutic drugs, including multiple sclerosis drug Betaferon.

Chief executive Giuseppe Vita said global sales in Betaferon, known as Betaseron in the United States, should rise by over 10 percent to 590 million marks even as competitor products, particularly U.S. group Biogen's Avonex, gained market share.

"We want to remain the market leader, but we will give up some market share to Avonex," Vita said. Schering had expected new competitors to erode its market dominance, enjoyed since it launched the product in the United States five years ago, he said.
Last year Betaferon sales reached 533 million marks.
The group's third key business segment, diagnostic products, was expected to show slower growth due to continuing price wars, particularly in Japan.

Schering was also currently benefiting from favourable exchange rates, something the group has been traditionally vulnerable to as it sells 85 percent of its products abroad, mostly in the United States and Japan.

"For the first time we can report that currencies barely had any impact (on 1996 results)," Pohle said. But while the dollar's stronger levels were positive, Schering still grappled with yen exchange rates.
As long as currency rates remained near current levels, Schering would continue to profit this year, said Pohle.
But recalling Schering's disaster year 1995 when the weak dollar seriously dented results, Pohle also warned that a drastic currency market change could affect Schering's outlook.
After making a splash with the Leiras and Jenapharm takeovers in 1996, Schering said it would be quite careful with any future moves, even as it remained interested in alliances.

"We would gladly make similar acquisitions like we made with Leiras and Jenapharm and we still have cash in our pockets," Pohle said. But prices for such companies had skyrocketed, outpacing their true value, he added.
Schering also brushed off talk it might itself be a takeover target, as Pohle said the 16.5 billion mark price tag was too high for most rivals.

Schering said the 1996 profits proved the group had recovered from a string of troubles in 1995 when it had to recall newly launched x-ray drug Isovist-280 and face health authority warnings that some of its pills could pose a health risk.
